items.title: Total War: SHOGUN 2 Complete Edition Review - The Best Total War Game Gets Even Better
items.author: James Lynch
items.summary: It's always a little weird going back to review a new version of a game that you've already played so much of for a number of reasons, not least because to
items.text:
It's always a little weird going back to review a new version of a game that you've already played so much of for a number of reasons, not least because to give it as fair of an appraisal as possible, you have to forget most of what came before. That's very difficult to do with Total War: Shogun 2, a game which got the franchise's signature formula down to a fine art.

When it first released back in 2011, it was also a bit of a technical marvel and it has held up remarkably well since, though the visuals of newer releases in the series have aged it a little. That's where the Complete Edition comes into play, a one-stop-shop for the base game and all of its DLC, all packaged with a bunch of technical advancements that are designed to thrust the game forward visually and mechanically.

In news that will likely come as a relief to those who have already sunk hundreds of hours into the original, the developer has done all of that with aplomb, and delivered what has to be the definitive Total War experience in the process.

Better Across The Board

The first thing to say about the game is that it looks absolutely spectacular, and right at home among the most recent comparable releases in the genre. The lighting and shadows add significant atmosphere to battle scenes, while the textures on the unit models, foliage on the world map, and scenery in general, all look considerably better.

Outside of the battle map, everything in the campaign has also been updated from a visual standpoint as well. The parchment campaign map, radar maps, loading screens and unit recruitment all look better, and tie in to the theme more closely, rather than being the more generic Total War efforts that they were before.

All of these efforts are underlined by the little differences that really show how much care and attention the development team have put into getting everything right. As an example, when the campaign map's seasonal changes occur, the whole world really does change, and the small details can be viewed by the player heading into Winter or Spring.

The game also features further nods to Japanese culture, which feels very appropriate given how much effort they have put into rendering this period of Japanese history. The coolest example of that (by some distance) is the new 2.5D movie style inspired by Japanese ukiyo-e art, while players can toggle between those and the classic movies in a further testament to how much choice this version of Shogun 2 provides.

A Campaign For The Ages

Anybody that plays Total War will know that the individual games in the series live and die by how well they deliver their main campaign. In the original Shogun 2's case, Creative Assembly really showed how this should be done, and this latest version makes tangible improvements while retaining the visual and mechanical identity that made it so spectacular in the first place.

The headline act this time around is the Realm Divide slider, which allows the mechanic to be retained, intensified or disabled entirely. The Realm Divide mechanic is an endgame system where the sitting Shogun notices what you've been up to and lives in fear of your potential power. This causes other AI clans to declare war on you in what becomes a conflagration for the ages. It's a ton of fun, but having the option to not force it to happen in every campaign run is a welcome change.

You also get a lot more options this time round from a campaign perspective, as the development team have made more than 50 minor factions playable for your next run (which were taken from options previously added by fan-made mods). Sure, it remains very fun to pick the Oda Clan and bulldoze through everyone in your path, but rising up as a smaller force and taking Japan for yourself is arguably more rewarding.

The battles within the campaign are also a lot closer to what the modern Total War player will be expecting going in, and while there is a world in which some might prefer the original, the changes made do seem sensible. They now include modern control options for moving units, while players also have access to birds-eye battle maps and overlays to better understand the landscape they'll be fighting in.

A Triumphant Experience

There have been other changes to the overall quality-of-life in the game as well, particularly via the implementation of fixes, some of which fans have been calling for. Fatigue now affects infantry combat statistics as well as morale, while balancing changes include Hattori and Tokugawa Kisho Ninjas now having improved statistics over normal Kisho Ninjas. At the same time, Mori port recruitment, ship fire chance in rain, campaign movement and unit spotting values have all been amended to make them as cogent as possible.

Many of the foibles that previously held the game back slightly have also been corrected, including ensuring that units receive the bonuses they are supposed to have, as well as campaign-effect interactions and Officer Assignments functioning as intended. There have also been a lot of accessibility changes, including color adjustment presets and separate voice and text language settings.

Lastly, the developer has taken a really admirable approach with mod support on this release, opening the game up to player creations while retaining all of the hard work that went into the original. Mod support for the original version of Shogun 2 will remain as is, allowing players to continue everything they have built up over the years.

At the same time, integrated Mod.io support is planned for the Complete Edition as it progresses, which should theoretically make it easier to mod than ever before. They haven't shared full details and mod integration information just yet, but we can expect to hear more about that shortly after launch.

All in all, Total War: Shogun 2 didn't have to do a lot to deliver a great game, considering just how competent its foundation is. That said, it really is impressive just how respect the development team has paid to the original, modernizing where needed while retaining that original essence that made it so magical in the first place.

It's a spectacular, enormous experience that strategy fans will undoubtedly be happy to play for hundreds of hours, and it should serve as the definitive introduction to the series for new fans moving forward. Is it the best Total War game of all time? Though I definitely have a soft spot for the original Rome release, it's fair to say that this is just about as good as it gets in the genre.

items.title: Steam Week in Review: The curious case of Wonder Boy in Monster Land's dubious PC debut
items.author: shaun.prescott@futurenet.com (Shaun Prescott)
items.summary: Wonder Boy in Monster Land released in Japanese arcades in 1987 and for the Sega Master System the following year. Its success led to numerous ports,
items.text:
Wonder Boy in Monster Land released in Japanese arcades in 1987 and for the Sega Master System the following year. Its success led to numerous ports, including to ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Atari ST. Oddly, it never received an official PC port, though that long absence appeared to have come to an end on September 28.

Did fans rejoice? Not really.

The Steam listing for Wonderboy in Monster Land raises one immediate red flag: note the rookie error of "Wonderboy" versus Wonder Boy. The developer and publisher is Retro Maniac, whose only other Steam game is Street Hoop, or Street Slam, an old Data East arcade game from 1994.

To bring you up to speed: LAT Corp owns all IP and assets once belonging to Westone Bit Entertainment, the creators of the original Wonder Boy games. But at the same time Sega, confusingly, owns the Wonder Boy trademark. In other words: LAT Corp owns the games, Sega owns the name. Both parties would need to OK any Wonder Boy re-release bearing the Wonder Boy name.

Box art for Wonder Boy in Monster Land on Master System (Image credit: Sega)While the "Wonderboy" misspelling is damning, a Wonder Boy game appearing on Steam without SEGA or LAT Corp prominently displayed isn't unusual. Wonder Boy Returns Remix, which is a "remake" of the original Wonder Boy, lists CFK Co., Ltd as developer and publisher. Not only was it officially licensed, but series creator Ryuichi Nishizawa was involved. Meanwhile, Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a thorough remake of the 1989 Master System original, developed by Lizardcube and published by Dotemu. It's also officially licensed. Each listing discloses as much in the Steam page fine print which appears under system requirements.

There's also the wider confusion around the name Wonder Boy itself, which reared its head with the release of Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom in 2019. Since rights to Wonder Boy games are split between LAT Corp and Sega it's necessary to get an OK from both to publish a Wonder Boy game with a Wonder Boy name. But what if you can only get the blessing of one? This dynamic was in play with Monster Boy, which is definitely, spiritually a Wonder Boy game—it had Nishizawa's handprints all over it—though publisher FDG Entertainment didn't license the Wonder Boy name from Sega, hence the name.

To confuse matters even more, the original arcade version of Wonder Boy released as Adventure Island in the United States, spawning a parallel line of unrelated follow-ups.

So what is a Wonder Boy game, then? Very few but diehards know off the top of their head, and if this new arcade "port" is illegitimate, it's probably released with full knowledge that this confusion will help it fly under the radar.

I wouldn't have thought twice about it if it weren't for the Wonder Boy Universe fan account on X, which raised the alarm on September 28. Composer on the original game, Shinichi Sakamoto, also weighed in, agreeing that the Retro Maniac port is illegitimate while pointing out that it's not available in Japan. (Sakamoto also claims it's been downloaded 10,000 times on Steam, though I don't know where he got that figure).

It turned out to be a problem that affected me directly. Apparently, it has already been downloaded 10,000 times on Steam. Yet, when accessing Steam from Japan, it doesn't show up—instead, you get a message saying, "This item is currently unavailable in your region."I am currently in the process of requesting its removal.September 29, 2026

Against my better judgement I bought and downloaded the alleged illegitimate version of Wonderboy in Monster Land, and can confirm it's simply a ROM running in the MAME arcade emulator (I've since requested a refund, which was issued promptly). The one obvious change is that a splash screen bearing the Sega logo has been removed.

The splash screen for the Retro Maniac version

The splash screen as depicted by YouTube channel Retro Fighters, playing an arcade ROM

(There's another variation depicted here, only Monster Land is in English rather than Japanese. The SEGA logo remains).

I reached out to Valve about the listing but didn't hear back. I also reached out to Sega several times but received no response. The Wonder Boy Universe X account claims the Retro Maniacs listing is "in the process of being DMCA'd by officials". Presumably they have a direct line to Sega or LAT that I don't have, because only Sega or LAT can file a DMCA. According to Valve's own documentation a DMCA complaint is processed in a maximum of 72 hours but can take longer if the situation is more complex.

Complex or not, Valve's documentation also shows what happens if your listing has a DMCA filed against it. Importantly, a public-facing notice will appear on the Steam page reading "A DMCA takedown notice has been filed on this item". That is yet to happen with Retro Maniac's listing.

This kind of thing happens a lot on mobile storefronts, especially for abandonware. But Wonder Boy in Monster Land isn't, at least strictly speaking, abandonware. I can't say I'm especially worried for Sega or LAT: it's obviously legally wrong for Retro Maniac to upload and profit from a game it didn't make or license—assuming that is the case—but Sega and LAT do themselves no favours by not having legitimate versions of Wonder Boy games easily available on Steam. Monster Lair and Monster World (but not Monster Land) used to be available as part of the SEGA Mega Drive and Genesis Classics collection, but that was removed from Steam in 2024.

Still, it's pretty funny how easily one can simply upload a rip off Wonder Boy game on Steam in 2026. A fortnight after its initial launch, Wonderboy in Monster Land is still officially available, and enthusiasts continue to wonder whether they should support it or not.

Also unsurprising is that it's currently sitting on "mixed" reviews. MMOs rarely or never launch to near-unanimous customer satisfaction, and the case against Aion 2 seems to be that it's structured like a free-to-play mobile game. The monetisation is apparently deep-rooted and endlessly distracting.

It's noteworthy that Minecraft Dungeons 2 only reached number ten during its first full week on sale. It's a Minecraft game, after all. It did launch onto Xbox Games Pass, and it's probably a better performer on console, but it still feels like a humble showing for an offshoot of one of the biggest games in the world.

Who needs parks, places to live, shops etcetera, when the land they inhabit would be better served by a car park? That's the dystopian premise of Car Park Capital, which has you destroying the world with vast stretches of yellow-lined tarmac. Here's a neat 'n' quiet driving game starring a big red truck and a world full of oddballs. And not only that, it was actually built for DVD: you can download the files, burn it to a disc, and experience it in its authentic environment. But what is it? "A game about nostalgia, escapism and what lurks inside 'dead' physical media," reads the Steam description. It has some arrestingly bizarre pixel art.

blocks.x: Wonder Boy in Monster Land released in Japanese arcades in 1987 and for the Sega Master System the following year. Its success led to numerous ports, including to ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Atari ST. Oddly, it never received an official PC port, though that long absence appeared to have come to an end on September 28.
Did fans rejoice? Not really.

The Steam listing for Wonderboy in Monster Land raises one immediate red flag: note the rookie error of "Wonderboy" versus Wonder Boy. The developer and publisher is Retro Maniac, whose only other Steam game is Street Hoop, or Street Slam, an old Data East arcade game from 1994.

To bring you up to speed: LAT Corp owns all IP and assets once belonging to Westone Bit Entertainment, the creators of the original Wonder Boy games. But at the same time Sega, confusingly, owns the Wonder Boy trademark. In other words: LAT Corp owns the games, Sega owns the name. Both parties would need to OK any Wonder Boy re-release bearing the Wonder Boy name.

Box art for Wonder Boy in Monster Land on Master System (Image credit: Sega)While the "Wonderboy" misspelling is damning, a Wonder Boy game appearing on Steam without SEGA or LAT Corp prominently displayed isn't unusual. Wonder Boy Returns Remix, which is a "remake" of the original Wonder Boy, lists CFK Co., Ltd as developer and publisher. Not only was it officially licensed, but series creator Ryuichi Nishizawa was involved. Meanwhile, Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a thorough remake of the 1989 Master System original, developed by Lizardcube and published by Dotemu. It's also officially licensed. Each listing discloses as much in the Steam page fine print which appears under system requirements.

There's also the wider confusion around the name Wonder Boy itself, which reared its head with the release of Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom in 2019. Since rights to Wonder Boy games are split between LAT Corp and Sega it's necessary to get an OK from both to publish a Wonder Boy game with a Wonder Boy name. But what if you can only get the blessing of one? This dynamic was in play with Monster Boy, which is definitely, spiritually a Wonder Boy game—it had Nishizawa's handprints all over it—though publisher FDG Entertainment didn't license the Wonder Boy name from Sega, hence the name.
To confuse matters even more, the original arcade version of Wonder Boy released as Adventure Island in the United States, spawning a parallel line of unrelated follow-ups.

So what is a Wonder Boy game, then? Very few but diehards know off the top of their head, and if this new arcade "port" is illegitimate, it's probably released with full knowledge that this confusion will help it fly under the radar.

I wouldn't have thought twice about it if it weren't for the Wonder Boy Universe fan account on X, which raised the alarm on September 28. Composer on the original game, Shinichi Sakamoto, also weighed in, agreeing that the Retro Maniac port is illegitimate while pointing out that it's not available in Japan. (Sakamoto also claims it's been downloaded 10,000 times on Steam, though I don't know where he got that figure).

It turned out to be a problem that affected me directly. Apparently, it has already been downloaded 10,000 times on Steam. Yet, when accessing Steam from Japan, it doesn't show up—instead, you get a message saying, "This item is currently unavailable in your region."I am currently in the process of requesting its removal.September 29, 2026

Against my better judgement I bought and downloaded the alleged illegitimate version of Wonderboy in Monster Land, and can confirm it's simply a ROM running in the MAME arcade emulator (I've since requested a refund, which was issued promptly). The one obvious change is that a splash screen bearing the Sega logo has been removed.
The splash screen for the Retro Maniac version
The splash screen as depicted by YouTube channel Retro Fighters, playing an arcade ROM
(There's another variation depicted here, only Monster Land is in English rather than Japanese. The SEGA logo remains).

I reached out to Valve about the listing but didn't hear back. I also reached out to Sega several times but received no response. The Wonder Boy Universe X account claims the Retro Maniacs listing is "in the process of being DMCA'd by officials". Presumably they have a direct line to Sega or LAT that I don't have, because only Sega or LAT can file a DMCA. According to Valve's own documentation a DMCA complaint is processed in a maximum of 72 hours but can take longer if the situation is more complex.

Complex or not, Valve's documentation also shows what happens if your listing has a DMCA filed against it. Importantly, a public-facing notice will appear on the Steam page reading "A DMCA takedown notice has been filed on this item". That is yet to happen with Retro Maniac's listing.

This kind of thing happens a lot on mobile storefronts, especially for abandonware. But Wonder Boy in Monster Land isn't, at least strictly speaking, abandonware. I can't say I'm especially worried for Sega or LAT: it's obviously legally wrong for Retro Maniac to upload and profit from a game it didn't make or license—assuming that is the case—but Sega and LAT do themselves no favours by not having legitimate versions of Wonder Boy games easily available on Steam. Monster Lair and Monster World (but not Monster Land) used to be available as part of the SEGA Mega Drive and Genesis Classics collection, but that was removed from Steam in 2024.

Still, it's pretty funny how easily one can simply upload a rip off Wonder Boy game on Steam in 2026. A fortnight after its initial launch, Wonderboy in Monster Land is still officially available, and enthusiasts continue to wonder whether they should support it or not.

items.author: Rick Lane

items.text:
One of the many ways AI will (supposedly) revolutionise the games industry in facilitating highly reactive NPCs via LLM-powered chatbots. Yet so far, only a handful of games like Where Winds Meet have attempted to implement the tech, and the results have been less than spectacular. But there might also be another reason why relatively few games feature LLM-powered NPCs, which is that powering such chatbots can be costly, as recently demonstrated by the developers of an upcoming driving instructor simulator

As reported by FRVR (via Kotaku) Teach My Little Sister How To Drive is a comic simulation game in which you coach your virtual sibling on driving technique from the comfort of the passenger seat. The twist is that behind your sister's dinner-plate eyes is an LLM chatbot (currently powered by an OpenAI model, though the developers intend to use Gemini for the final release) In the role of instructor, players can both converse with the chatbot and issue vocal instructions such as "turn left here", to which the bot will respond accordingly. At least, that's the theory.

Developer Easy Fox released a demo for Teach My Little Sister How To Drive back in February, but in the past month the game has seen a surge in players, which has had an interesting knock-on effect for the demo. "The number of demo players has grown more than twentyfold," Easy Fox explained in a Steam post, adding. "This growth has also increased our operating costs considerably."

Easy Fox goes on to explain that it is "spending over $1,000 per day on AI services for the demo", as players burn through tokens prompting the LLM by proxy. Easy Fox claims that figure "isn't because each player is particularly expensive to support", but rather that "so many people are playing."

As a result of this, Easy Fox has "taken out a bank loan to help keep the demo running". Yet even this may not be sufficient to support the demo long term. "Financial pressure may mean we have to close the demo earlier than expected before the full release," Easy Fox says, though the studio stresses it has "not made that decision at this time".

According to FRVR, that twentyfold increase in players amounts to 450 concurrent. While the overall player numbers will be higher than that, it isn't an enormous figure, and it makes me wonder how financially viable the game will be when it is released. Easy Fox says it will "account for expected AI usage in the game's price". But it also says that players "will not be charged separately for their individual AI token usage after purchasing the game".

That might work in the short term, but surely those token costs are going to pile up over time. It's also worth noting that AI token costs are highly unpredictable, with even large companies like Microsoft and Uber struggling to accurately predict the cost and burn rate of their own internal token use. In its Steam post, Easy Fox says it's looking into options like introducing local AI models for players with "sufficiently capable GPUs". But that's only going to be a fraction of the player-base.

All of this is aside from whether an AI-powered driving instruction game is a good idea. Personally, I think the fact that it revolves specifically around chatting with another character makes this a more sensible application than in Where Winds Meet, where the chatbots don't factor into the game design in any meaningful way. It's much more reminiscent of early chatbot-based social sim Façade.

But the very fact it reminds me of Façade makes me wonder whether the game needs a premium LLM connected to it to achieve its goal. Easy Fox states that current design problems being addressed include "dialogue that feels too artificial and breaks immersion" and "commands being carried out incorrectly, such as turning right when asked to turn left." All of which seems like it could be solved with a good voice actor and a sufficiently rich dialogue system. Easy Fox plans to release the full game in January next year, so we'll find out exactly how the finances stack up then.

items.title: “Cupertino” is a Smart Big Tech Procedural
items.author: Jen Chaney
items.summary: Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s
items.text:
Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg (“The Social Reckoning”), Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (“You Can See Everything”), Elon Musk (Alex Gibney’s “Musk”), and OpenAI’s Sam Altman (“Artificial”). Television is in on the trend, too. In November, Netflix will remind us of the implosion of cryptocurrency fund FTX and its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, in “The Altruists.”

On CBS and Paramount+ starting Thursday, there’s “Cupertino,” a broadcast-network procedural that doesn’t zero in on a real-life tech bro, but does raise a lot of sobering questions about the industry currently attempting to cram A.I. down the throats of the global populace.

Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

“I’m sick of people controlling my fate, and my guess is there are a lot of people out there that feel the same way but don’t have anyone to represent them,” says Michael Price (Mike Colter of “Luke Cage” and “Evil”), an attorney who co-founded, then got edged out of, an extremely successful big tech company called S-Talk.

He’s explaining his reasons for wanting to start an agency that takes on the cases against Magnificent 7-level companies that other firms are too afraid to touch. But he could just as easily be describing this show’s appeal to an American audience frustrated by the unemployment rate, the disproportionate power and wealth of the billionaire class, and the non-stop insistence that everyone get on board with artificial intelligence.

Unlike the other projects mentioned above, “Cupertino” does not focus on the idiosyncrasies/neuroses of a single, perceived “genius.” It is more general in its depiction of big tech, which enables it to feel both timely and, perhaps, more relatable to the average person.

Pictured (L-R): Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre and Mike Colter as Michael Price. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved.

While there are some key storylines that run throughout the first 10 episodes—the rivalry between Michael and his showboating lawyer father (Joe Morton); another, separate rivalry between Michael and his ex, also an attorney (Renée Elise Goldsberry, who co-starred opposite Colter on “Evil”); and, most importantly, an ongoing narrative about a particularly dangerous form of AI—this is largely a case-of-the-week type of show.

With its quick, plot-driven pacing, “Cupertino” is episodic, mainstream network storytelling that shows, like so much of the Kings’ output, that it’s still possible to make smart, sophisticated, digestible television within that framework.

As Michael, Colter is dignified, pragmatic and, if I’m being honest, not wildly different in demeanor from David, the priest the actor played on “Evil.” But he’s a persuasive lead in both shows, so I’m not going to complain too much about any overlap. While Michael believes in justice and the rule of law, he’s not some anti-capitalist hero who wants to burn down all of Silicon Valley. He simply sees a gap in the marketplace that needs filling. “When you’re in the middle of the ocean, you don’t sell people more water,” he explains to Goldsberry’s Nichole. “You sell them life jackets.”

His partner at the new firm, Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), a devout Christian and gifted lawyer who also gets fired from S-Talk after being sexually harassed by the head of the company, is the bleeding heart in this pairing. Keller and Colter have an organic, friendly chemistry that, to the show’s credit, is supportive without being romantic, at least not in these early episodes.

But the standout performances in “Cupertino” come from the two actors who provide the most comedic relief in a drama that doesn’t shy away from poking fun at the always-pitching culture of venture capitalism. Ella Stiller (daughter of Ben Stiller and Christine Taylor) gets a break-out role as Christy Palladino, a third employee who gets fired from S-Talk and becomes the receptionist at Price and Siffre, where she proves to be a fantastic investigator for her attorney bosses.

Christy is particularly adept at tracking down leads and calling in favors from her extensive family of blue-collar workers; after being escorted out of the S-Talk building, she phones her electrician uncle, who proceeds to turn the power on and off in that office and enrage everyone still “lucky” enough to be employed there. Christy knows nothing about technology, but she loves to stick it to the man. Her default expression is resting “you’ve got to be kidding me” face, and Stiller has got that expression down pat.

Pictured (L-R): Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved

Then there’s Busy Phillips, who’s cast as Natalia Boutella, a key investor in the new firm who also happens to be divorced from a tech executive played by Fisher Stevens who is not Jeff Bezos, but also is totally Jeff Bezos. Natalia is less interested in sticking it to the man than she is in sticking it to that particular man. When he denies that he has gained weight after she tells him he “got fat,” Natalia counters: “You dined with the president, you had a front row seat to that inauguration, you bought a billion-dollar yacht. You got fat.” Phillips utters lines like that as if they’re coated in venom.

(As an added bonus, every time she and Goldsberry appear in the same scene, it’s like a partial “Girls5Eva” reunion, and that alone deserves a fresh designation on Rotten Tomatoes.)

The Kings and co. tackle numerous zeitgeisty tech trends; one episode focuses on a teenager compelled to kill his father by a chatbot, while another, which happens to debut less than a week before the midterms, zeroes in on prediction websites used to manipulate elections.

But “Cupertino” is not a purely anti-A.I. narrative. The episodes also highlight situations where technological assistance can help. In one, Christy gets incredibly frustrated by an A.I. agent she attempts to train by making sure its knowledge of horror movies is up to snuff. (“In which state did ‘The Blair Witch Project‘ take place?” she asks. “Wisconsin,” the agent cheerfully responds. Christy: “No, Maryland, moron.”) But she’s pretty grateful for that moron when he can warn her not to take a sip of a drink that’s been spiked at a bar.

If “Cupertino” has an official position on technology, it’s that it can be very useful, but it desperately needs significant, legally enforceable guardrails. This is an opinion shared by most sentient beings with anything akin to a conscience. This series dares to suggest that there’s a world where guardrails could be put in place, and where the “little guys” in the tech world have a chance to be heard. Maybe that’s a fantasy, but it’s one that’s extremely entertaining to live in for 42 minutes every week.

The first ten episodes of season one were screened in advance for critics. An additional ten episodes are currently in production.

When he denies that he has gained weight after she tells him he “got fat,” Natalia counters: “You dined with the president, you had a front row seat to that inauguration, you bought a billion-dollar yacht. You got fat.” Phillips utters lines like that as if they’re coated in venom.
(As an added bonus, every time she and Goldsberry appear in the same scene, it’s like a partial “Girls5Eva” reunion, and that alone deserves a fresh designation on Rotten Tomatoes.)

The Kings and co. tackle numerous zeitgeisty tech trends; one episode focuses on a teenager compelled to kill his father by a chatbot, while another, which happens to debut less than a week before the midterms, zeroes in on prediction websites used to manipulate elections.

But “Cupertino” is not a purely anti-A.I. narrative. The episodes also highlight situations where technological assistance can help. In one, Christy gets incredibly frustrated by an A.I. agent she attempts to train by making sure its knowledge of horror movies is up to snuff. (“In which state did ‘The Blair Witch Project‘ take place?” she asks. “Wisconsin,” the agent cheerfully responds. Christy: “No, Maryland, moron.”) But she’s pretty grateful for that moron when he can warn her not to take a sip of a drink that’s been spiked at a bar.

If “Cupertino” has an official position on technology, it’s that it can be very useful, but it desperately needs significant, legally enforceable guardrails. This is an opinion shared by most sentient beings with anything akin to a conscience. This series dares to suggest that there’s a world where guardrails could be put in place, and where the “little guys” in the tech world have a chance to be heard. Maybe that’s a fantasy, but it’s one that’s extremely entertaining to live in for 42 minutes every week.
The first ten episodes of season one were screened in advance for critics. An additional ten episodes are currently in production.

items.text:
I blink and I've somehow spent another 30 hours in Shogun 2. Undoubtedly my favorite of the older Total War games—and I don't say that lightly as someone who also has big hour counts in Rome and Medieval 2—there's just something so straightforward about the second Shogun; an elegant simplicity complimented by a period where the Creative Assembly was clearly having fun experimenting with all sorts of ideas.

It's no wonder it chose to remaster the game despite the fact it's arguably the best aged Total War there is. I'd happily go back and play Shogun 2 over Rome 2, or even Attila, which I think speaks to how well it holds up. It's definitely nice to play Shogun 2 with improved visuals (if you like the new style), modern unit controls, and full Japanese voice acting, but I think Creative Assembly missed the mark in terms of the remaster's other additions.

To give it a fair shot, I started with one of the newly introduced island-bound minor factions, Honma. I always love conquering this island in campaigns because they have a gold mine, plus starting on an island in the north adds loads of possibilities. The first thing I noticed, though, is that none of the 50 new minor factions in Shogun 2's campaigns get unique bonuses, which would've gone a long way to distinguishing them from the minor faction unlocker mods Shogun 2 already had.

(Image credit: Creative Assembly)Without any passive bonuses to define playstyle, or tweaks to every faction starting with the same units, location is the only differential for these clans. I also discovered that the trade system hasn't been updated to account for single-region island factions, meaning my beloved Honma was only able to trade with one faction for the entirety of the campaign. Again, a QoL tweak would have made sense there.

In terms of the additions you'll actually feel in your campaigns, the new "Realm Divide" difficulty options for the endgame, improved visuals and terrain, and reworked unit controls are really the standout features—I went back to the original Shogun 2 afterwards, and the battlefield visual differences are notable. But the bird's eye battle view? The region overlay? I didn't use either of these once. The diplomatic quick deal is another somewhat useless addition. You don't form alliances or trade agreements anywhere near often enough in Shogun 2 to necessitate quick deal (as with Total War: Warhammer's 100s of factions), but the feature also doesn't include "arrange marriage".

(Image credit: Creative Assembly)A way to easily find out which factions had spousal candidates is the one diplomatic QoL change I genuinely would've found useful. While I did enjoy my campaign as Honma, I kept running into new QoL problems the original had that the remaster could have solved. No ability to merge units, for example, which would've been great in a game as attritional as Shogun 2, where unit upkeep isn't affected by remaining soldiers. Perhaps a numerical indicator for units in your army, which would save you counting them each time?

Shogun 2 still plays well, but that's not contingent on this remaster

What about agents accompanying armies getting left behind in settlements or on ships? Or how enlisted generals always appear back at your capital? I could go on, but there are so many QoL improvements this remaster could have made to Shogun 2 without infringing on the identity of the game. Even wider issues like siege pathfinding, which can still be dreadful, or problems with enemy AI.

I had one battle in the remaster where the besieging enemy general ran up to my wall, and then sat there for 40 minutes as I fast forwarded (a known bug I never even experienced in the original game). Or how about fixing the overly defensive naval AI, which sees you having to cross the entire map every battle just to engage enemy ships. You can see a full list of bug fixes for Shogun 2 - Complete Edition and it's not particularly extensive considering players have had 15 years to document every busted element, and I haven't even mentioned multiplayer bugs like the desync issue.

Yes, Shogun 2 still plays well, and I absolutely recommend it to Total War or strategy fans, but that's not contingent on this remaster. All the things that were great before are still great, whether it's battling with samurai to become shogun, or unloading a line of rifle infantry and cannon into enemy armies in Fall of the Samurai If anything, I believe Shogun 2's quality as a game deserved a better and more extensive reworking than it's been given.

At least Shogun 2's DLC factions, who are now free, like the Christian Otomo, religious rebel Ikko-Ikki, or cannon-toting Saga in Fall of the Samurai, are some of the spiciest campaigns if you've never played them, and a whole bunch of people will get to try them for the first time (if they missed when those were previously free).

Any reason to return to Shogun 2 in 2026 is something to be celebrated, but I just wish Complete Edition felt more extensive and essential versus leaving so much undone. If you own Shogun 2 already, you'll get a month-long 75% discount when the game launches on Steam on October 13, while owners of the original will get all the legacy faction DLC for free, as mentioned.

items.author: Hannah Hunt

items.text:
The Walking Dead has spent years proving that surviving the initial outbreak is only the beginning of the problem. Eventually, someone needs food, the supplies run out, and the supposedly secure place everyone has settled into stops looking so secure. Getting through another day often depends on a decision that seems perfectly reasonable until someone opens the wrong door.

Watching those decisions unfold also makes it very easy to believe you could do better. Surely you wouldn’t waste ammunition, leave a perfectly good shelter, or risk everyone’s lives over a supply run that could have waited. Halloween offers a good excuse to test that confidence, especially for viewers who have spent years insisting they’d last longer than the people on television.

Project Zomboid is giving plenty of players that opportunity, recording a 24-hour peak of 64,086 concurrent players on October 9, according to Steam Charts. The Indie Stone’s zombie survival game has also averaged 50,069 concurrent players over the past 30 days. That’s a substantial audience for a title approaching the thirteenth anniversary of its November 8, 2013, Steam release, and it follows an even bigger summer for the long-running survival hit.

‘Project Zomboid’ Is Still Drawing Huge Crowds Ahead of Halloween

Image via The Indie Stone

Project Zomboid reached its all-time concurrent peak of 124,506 players in August, when its monthly average climbed above 76,000. Activity has cooled since then, with the rolling 30-day average down approximately 8%, but it remains well above July’s average of roughly 30,000. The October figures show that the game is maintaining a sizable audience after that record-breaking month, even as the initial rush subsides. For The Walking Dead fans, the premise should sound familiar. Set in a zombie-infested region of Kentucky, Project Zomboid asks players to scavenge supplies and establish somewhere safe enough to survive. Hunger and illness can become problems long before a zombie reaches the front door, while the eventual loss of electricity makes getting comfortable a dangerous assumption. A gun can help with an immediate threat, but the noise can also bring more trouble.

Playing with friends adds another complication. Players can survive alone or join others online, turning questions about supplies and safety into decisions everyone has to live with. Knowing when to abandon a plan matters just as much as making one, particularly when another player’s mistake can put the group at risk. Anyone who spent entire episodes questioning Rick’s leadership now has an opportunity to see how their own holds up. The player response remains strong alongside those attendance figures. The game’s Steam listing shows 91% positive reviews over the past 30 days, earning a “Very Positive” recent rating.

Project Zomboid is still available in Early Access, with no announced release date for version 1.0.

items.text:
Welcome to What’s On, our weekly roundup of notable shows. Here is what’s happening on TV from Sunday, October 11 to Saturday, October 17. All times are Eastern.


Treasure Island (MGM+, Sunday, 10 p.m., series premiere) An action-packed reimagining of Robert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel of the same name, this six-episode British miniseries follows 18th-century teenager Jim Hawkins (Tom Sweet) and his formidable mother Bess (Hayley Atwell), who come into possession of an old treasure map and get dragged into a deadly race for Captain Flint’s buried gold. Voyaging aboard The Hispaniola, the mother-son duo navigate threats from both infamous pirate Long John Silver (David Oyelowo) and revolutionary spy Aaron Graham (Jack Huston). Look for The A.V. Club’s review on Monday.


VisionQuest (Disney+, Wednesday, 9 p.m., series premiere) Concluding the trilogy that kicked off with 2021’s WandaVision and continued with 2024’s Agatha All Along, this MCU miniseries picks up with Paul Bettany’s Vision living in hiding after escaping from government forces. When a bounty is placed on his head, however, he sets off with a mysterious teen named Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica) as well as his collection of internal AI personas, including the powerful supervillain Ultron (voiced by James Spader). Elizabeth Olsen is reportedly not returning as the Scarlet Witch, but Todd Stashwick, T’Nia Miller, Emily Hampshire, and James D’Arcy also star. Watch for The A.V. Club’s pre-air review in the coming days, with recaps starting Wednesday night.


Crystal Lake (Peacock, Thursday, series premiere) A prequel to the Friday The 13th film franchise, this eight-episode slasher series digs into the bloody 1970s origins of the Voorhees family, led by single mom Pam (Linda Cardellini). Mourning the death of her only son—the future hockey mask-wearing murderer Jason (Callum Vinson), who drowned at the titular summer camp—Pam desperately clings to the belief that her boy is still alive. However, her grief is disrupted when the town’s chief of police (William Catlett) and his journalist sister (Devin Kessler) begin investigating unusual deaths in the area and uncovering Pam’s troubled past. We’ll have our review of the series Tuesday.

Norm: The Tale Of Norm Macdonald (Netflix, Friday, documentary premiere) The master of deadpan humor gets an affectionate bio-doc from director Judd Apatow, who lets the titular late comedian and Saturday Night Live icon narrate his own story. Using rare home videos, personal photos and archival footage, the film traces Macdonald’s life and career, from his roots in rural Canada and early stand-up days to his iconic “Weekend Update” era (and subsequent firing) and beyond. Macdonald has a long-standing reputation as a “comic’s comic,” so it’s not a shock to see the participation of peers like David Letterman, Sarah Silverman, Jim Carrey, Adam Sandler, and David Spade throughout the doc.

The Rainmaker (USA Network, Friday, 10 p.m., season two premiere)


Ending soon

items.text:
The descent into autumn continues: this week I slept with an extra blanket on the bed. I'm not into swapping the duvet out for the winter tog yet, I'll be holding off on that until at least December, but the laying of the first blanket is a true marker of autumn's arrival.

Another change I was telling the team about to definitely rapt fascination was that I've brought the dehumidifier out to reduce condensation in the living room when drying washing. Not only that, I'm combining it with the fan I bought in summer to keep the air circulating. Reader, I don't mean to boast, but it dried two loads of washing including heavy ply towels overnight.

But enough about my successes, this is what the rest of the team are up to.

Edwin
This weekend I'll be checking out the demo for Ablahshikar, a turn-based ship-salvaging game with ASCII art and some extremely extra writing. As the developers put it: "Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." Ta to former RPS scribe and current Steam Hype editor Dominic Tarason for passing it on.

Mark
I've got another mystery game I'm slowly chipping away at. When I'm not on with that I might finally get around to checking out The Witcher 3's new coat of paint. I just need to double check I've not got any residue left over from a previous modded installation where I'd turned Gerry into a man-torsoed and horse-legged centaur, since that might cause the new version of the all-timer RPG to get a bit confused. I'm also due a return to Star Wars: Galactic Racer for a proper taste of its multiplayer now the podracing gates have opened to everyone.

Ollie
This weekend I'll be away from my... well, not my PC, because that's still borked. But my PC setup. Which is an important distinction, because for the time being I've been plugging my two monitors and all my peripherals into my laptop and playing on there, to varying degrees of success. But this weekend I'm travelling, so I've packed up said laptop - and also brought along my Steam Deck, my Steam Frame, and my Steam Controller. No, I'm not sponsored. I just don't know what I want to play or how I want to play it.

James
Wait, Ollie has a Steam Frame? At last, a second person I know who does. On a related note, there's a Titanfall 2 VR mod I've been meaning to try, and am finally free enough from review duties to make the time for it.

Jeremy
I'm playing an upcoming game that involves exploring a very large area, attacking things, and occasionally eating big pieces of chicken. You commentators who have been following my WAPs recently will figure it out.

Callum
Upon learning it was his one year anniversary at RPS, Callum announced he was departing for the sewers to "make good on the pact". We wish him good luck.

Julian
No doubt I will be hanging up more washing and testing this fan/dehumidifier system to check it wasn't just a fluke. But, if that doesn't take up all my time, I will also be playing some Dorfromantik. I've had my eye on it for a while but after talking to the Volatiles devs about it's tile placing mechanic I was convinced to finally buy it.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

items.title: Ambitious “Control Resonant” Challenges Expectations, Rewards Creativity
items.author: Brian Tallerico

items.text:
Even though people often love to point out this site’s namesake’s opinion on video games, since we began this coverage, we’ve tried to write about where the form intersects with film in cinematic franchises like “Silent Hill,” “Uncharted,” and “Resident Evil.” While playing the absolutely brilliant “Control Resonant,” I kept thinking of some of the most ambitious, game-changing science fiction films of all time, obvious influences like “The Matrix” and “Inception.”

But I also found myself pondering the work of David Lynch. How do “Twin Peaks” and Remedy Entertainment’s masterpiece intersect? It’s in a creator’s willingness to push boundaries, to use the visual language of dreams, and to find emotional grounding in the impossible. Creative Director Mikael Kasurinen has said via the review guide, “We wanted to make something that provokes. Something that feels like nothing you’ve played before.” Mission accomplished.

The excellent “Control” ended with hero Jesse Faden finding her brother Dylan, cleansing him of the infection by the all-powerful Hiss, and leaving him and the place known as The Oldest House under lockdown. Jesse became the Director of the FBC (Federal Bureau of Control) and promised to figure out a way to fix whatever had broken reality in New York City, allowing enemies from an extradimensional space to invade Gotham. Come to think of it: With its reality-shaking vision of Lovecraftian creatures that might literally be from Hell, “Control” has a bit of “Event Horizon” in its DNA, too.

Seven years after the Hiss invaded the Oldest House, Jesse wakes up Dylan and promptly disappears. Dylan becomes the hero of “Resonant,” which is one of many elements that give it a different aesthetic from its predecessor. One thing that takes a bit of getting used to is that this is not “Control 2” for a reason. It is a very different experience, trading the tight location work of the Oldest House for open-world gameplay with multiple zones and far more freedom of choice.

Early in “Resonant,” Dylan aligns with an FBC agent named Zoe de Vera, a companion who speaks to Dylan through the PS5 controller. You work with Zoe to figure out how an event called the “Patterning” has divided New York City from reality, leading to the invasion by thousands of creatures that want Dylan dead. As in many open-world games, you’re free to roam as Dylan, though the developers brilliantly layer in new powers for Faden that unlock new regions, combat approaches, and different enemies. The game balances wiping out packs of routine enemies, the occasional fight with a Resonant or boss, and alternating story and main missions.

The “Resonant” developers lean into significantly more RPG elements with Dylan than they did with Jesse. Skill trees, magical items, various weapons to choose for a loadout—it’s all deeply customizable. That said, combat works similarly no matter the angle you take. It’s mostly melee-based combat with a steady flow of strike-and-dodge mechanics, but you can also unlock special powers through game progress, including summoning allies to fight alongside you and hurling projectiles.

My first few hours with “Resonant” were mixed. It truly does require you to recalibrate expectations after the relatively linear first game. I found myself wandering New York City, unsure what to do and wondering why the story missions were kicking my ass. The answer is that this game doesn’t just encourage exploration; it requires it. You can’t push through only the story missions in “Resonant” because you won’t be strong enough. You need to complete side missions to level up and become strong enough to take on enemies like Resonants, but you also need to explore the city, wandering into places like laundromats and gyms to find upgrade resources.

After a couple of hours, “Resonant” kicks into gear and doesn’t look back. Several missions in this game rank among the best of the last several years, including one where you escape a sinkhole and one where Dylan plays with shadows of himself and a younger Jesse that are unquestionably moving. This game does things narratively that would terrify most writers’ rooms in games, TV, or film. The missions can be so wildly unpredictable—one minute you’re guiding a magical cat to fight a demon and the next you’re battling mold spore creatures that look like the kin of Bloaters from “The Last of Us.”

You can never quite tell where “Resonant” is going, which gives it the storytelling power of great film or television. It’s got enough authorial decisions through customization and exploration to make you feel like you’re in “Control,” but it also contains remarkably confident writing, not just in plot but dialogue and character work as well.

And then there’s the navigation. After a few clunky hours where even getting around NYC can feel tough, Dylan gains two powers: one that can pull him to points on buildings above him, and one that can basically turn the entire world on its axis. You know that scene in “Inception” wherein Elliot Page’s character flips the city on itself and they “walk up” a street?

Now imagine that in gameplay. While it sounds almost impossibly disorienting, the developers use it in just the right places, allowing Dylan to control not just through superpowered combat but by shifting the entire world around him. It leads to some of the most stunning level design in years, especially late in the game when the entire setting becomes pliable.

What Remedy Entertainment is doing with the “Alan Wake” and “Control” games is unlike anything else on the market. They’re accomplishing what so many great artists have done: Pushing back against the rules and expectations put on their form by so many years of conforming creators. We can argue all day about the definitions of art, but the ambition in “Control Resonant” is a sibling of what we so often look for in literature, film, or theatre, too. It’s that charge we all get when we can tell something is working in a way we haven’t really experienced before. Maybe more than any game this year, “Resonant” has it.

The Publisher provided a review copy of this title. It is now available on PS5, Xbox Series, and Windows.

items.text:
Rami Malek's 'John Wick' Replacement Is Officially a Prime Video Favorite

Image via 20th Century Studios

Published Oct 12, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

2026 has had the biggest summer in the short careers to date of real-life married couple Tom Holland and Zendaya. Not only did they both feature in Christopher Nolan's ambitious historical epic The Odyssey, which is currently the front-runner to take the Best Picture title and numerous other prizes at the Academy Awards next year, but they also both returned in the biggest film of the decade so far: Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The latest MCU blockbuster saw Holland and Zendaya return as Peter Parker and MJ, respectively, in a film that not only stole the hearts of long-time Spidey fans but also smashed all box office expectations. Of all its many box office achievements, the most impressive is becoming the highest-grossing film ever at the domestic box office, with a domestic haul that surpassed the $950 million mark. But Zendaya and Holland weren't the only actors to appear in both these huge 2026 blockbusters, as they did so alongside Jon Bernthal.

Bernthal's 2026 has been busy beyond these two hits, also starring in the surprise Netflix hit His & Hers, Marvel’s Special Presentation, The Punisher: One Last Kill, and the return of Christopher Storer’s The Bear. As the dust settles on a massive year for Bernthal, and he enjoys a well-earned break, his presence on the streaming charts is still impressive. At the time of writing, Bernthal's underrated 2025 spy thriller The Amateur is one of the ten most-streamed movies on Prime Video in the U.S., a list topped by Now You See Me: Now You Don’t, a heist threequel that features fellow Brand New Day alum Mark Ruffalo.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Coen Brothers Movie Would You Thrive In?
Lebowski · O Brother · Fargo · No Country

Nobody writes people like the Coen brothers. The decent ones. The talkers. The ones who stopped trying years ago. And the ones who can already see how bad this is going to get. Four films, four completely different ways of handling trouble. Eight questions decide which one you would actually walk out of.

🎳Lebowski(1998)

🎸O Brother(2000)

❄️Fargo(1996)

🪙No Country(2007)

FIND YOUR FILM →

01

A bag of money lands in your lap. What happens next?
Every Coen film starts roughly here. It never goes smoothly.

AI do not overthink it. Rent is paid, evening is free.
BI have a plan for this. It involves other people.
CI hand it in. Somebody is looking for this.
DI am gone before anyone knows I have it.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Somebody is being completely unreasonable with you. How does it go?
Coen dialogue is mostly people failing to understand each other.

AI let it go. It is not worth the energy.
BI talk. At length. Until they are on my side.
CI stay polite and repeat myself until they hear me.
DI stop talking. Talking has not been working.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What is your actual relationship with work?
Everyone in these films is either working far too hard or not at all.

AI have arranged things so I do as little as possible.
BI would rather chase one big idea than hold a steady job.
CI do it properly, including the boring parts.
DIt pays. I do not need it to mean anything.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Long drive, bad weather, nobody else on the road. How are you?
There is always a drive in these films. It is never a good drive.

AMusic on, in no hurry, perfectly content.
BTalking the whole way, whether anybody answers or not.
CBoth hands on the wheel, checking everyone is warm enough.
DQuiet, watching the mirrors.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

You are offered a shortcut that is not quite legal.
This is the moment where the Coens find out who you really are.

ANo, but not on principle. It sounds like effort.
BYes, and I will make it sound like a great idea.
CNo. And I would probably say something about it.
DOnly if I am certain nobody finds out.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

The plan has fallen apart completely. What is your move?
In a Coen film the plan always falls apart. That is the genre.

AOrder a drink and let things settle down.
BImprovise loudly and hope momentum carries it.
CStart again from the beginning and do it right.
DCut my losses and leave before it gets worse.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Which of these sounds most like something you would say?
Nobody writes a line quite like the Coens. Which one is yours?

AIt is really not that serious.
BTrust me, I have thought about this.
CI just think we could all be a bit kinder.
DThat was always going to happen.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

How does your film end?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your movie.

ANothing is resolved and I am completely fine with it.
BA ridiculous piece of luck saves everybody.
CQuietly, at home, with somebody I love.
DSomebody older admits they no longer understand the world.

REVEAL MY FILM →

The Verdict Is In
Your Coen Film Is…

Four films, four completely different ways of handling money, trouble
and other people. This is the one you would survive, why it suits you, and what it would cost you to
be there.

The Big Lebowski · 1998

The Big Lebowski

You have quietly arranged your life so that very little can get
to you, and a surprising number of people find that infuriating. You would be completely at
home here.

The Dude is the only person in the film with no ambition, and the only one who comes out
the other side undamaged. That is not an accident.

You do not chase things. You let situations arrive and you deal with them at your own
pace, which is a genuine skill however lazy it looks.

This is a full crime plot happening around a man who mostly wants his rug back, and that
is exactly the energy you would bring to it.

Everything goes wrong. You abide. The film ends.

O Brother, Where Art Thou? · 2000

O Brother

You talk your way through life and it works far more often than
it should. Give you a bad situation and an audience and you will find a way out of both at
once.

Everett never has a plan that survives contact with reality. He has something better,
which is the ability to keep talking until a new one turns up.

You are the optimist in the group, the one who makes a ridiculous idea sound reasonable
at two in the morning.

This is the warmest film the Coens have made. It is a chase, a comedy and a musical at
once, and nobody in it is quite beyond saving.

You would end up famous entirely by accident, and act like you planned it all along.

Fargo · 1996

Fargo

You would survive Fargo because you are the only kind of person
who does: patient, decent, and completely unimpressed by anybody trying to be clever.

Marge Gunderson solves the whole case by being polite, thorough and unhurried while
everybody around her panics. That is the entire argument of the film.

You do the boring parts of the job, which is precisely why you would notice the thing
everyone else walked straight past.

Fargo is about ordinary greed causing enormous damage, and about one person who simply
refuses to be corrupted by any of it.

You would go home at the end of it, have dinner, and sleep perfectly well.

No Country for Old Men · 2007

No Country

You do not expect the world to be fair and you stopped being
surprised about it a long time ago. That clear-eyed quality is exactly what this film asks
for.

No Country is the Coens at their coldest: a film where being smart, fast and careful
might still not be anywhere near enough.

You plan for the worst, you keep your own counsel, and some part of you is already
working out the exit.

Llewelyn Moss is competent, prepared and resourceful, and the film is honest about
whether any of that is ever sufficient.

You would see it coming. Whether that helps is the one question the film refuses to
answer.

2026 has had the biggest summer in the short careers to date of real-life married couple Tom Holland and Zendaya. Not only did they both feature in Christopher Nolan's ambitious historical epic The Odyssey, which is currently the front-runner to take the Best Picture title and numerous other prizes at the Academy Awards next year, but they also both returned in the biggest film of the decade so far: Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The latest MCU blockbuster saw Holland and Zendaya return as Peter Parker and MJ, respectively, in a film that not only stole the hearts of long-time Spidey fans but also smashed all box office expectations. Of all its many box office achievements, the most impressive is becoming the highest-grossing film ever at the domestic box office, with a domestic haul that surpassed the $950 million mark. But Zendaya and Holland weren't the only actors to appear in both these huge 2026 blockbusters, as they did so alongside Jon Bernthal.

Bernthal's 2026 has been busy beyond these two hits, also starring in the surprise Netflix hit His & Hers, Marvel’s Special Presentation, The Punisher: One Last Kill, and the return of Christopher Storer’s The Bear. As the dust settles on a massive year for Bernthal, and he enjoys a well-earned break, his presence on the streaming charts is still impressive. Your Coen Film Is…

Four films, four completely different ways of handling money, trouble

The Big Lebowski

You have quietly arranged your life so that very little can get
to you, and a surprising number of people find that infuriating. You would be completely at

The Dude is the only person in the film with no ambition, and the only one who comes out
the other side undamaged. That is not an accident.

You do not chase things. You let situations arrive and you deal with them at your own
pace, which is a genuine skill however lazy it looks.
